subject: Business
source: Edexcel GCSE Business (1BS0) specification, Theme 2: Building a business, section 2.1 Growing the business (organic and external growth, financing growth, changes in aims, globalisation, ethics and the environment); retrieval starters draw on Theme 1 which is assumed taught in Year 10. The school Drive holds only an AQA 8132 scheme of work and legacy topic folders, used for activity ideas only; all content written to the Edexcel specification and subject knowledge. Business examples are fictional unless stated | Edexcel 4BS1 specification (headline content for units 2.3-2.5, 3.1-3.5, 5.1-5.4, 1.5-1.8). The older UK GCSE 1BS0 lessons in content/lessons/business/y11.json already cover economies and diseconomies of scale, globalisation, trade barriers and ethics for the old board; this set re-teaches 5.1 and 1.5 only with 4BS1-specific content (exchange-rate calculations, multinationals and host countries) and IGCSE-style questions.

lessons.title: Why and how businesses grow: organic growth
objectives: Explain why businesses want to grow and how growth can be measured
Describe organic growth and assess its advantages and disadvantages

keywords.def: an increase in the size of a business, such as sales, staff or outlets
growth from within the business using its own resources and sales
growth by joining with or buying another business
a business's sales as a percentage of total market sales
to sell new types of product or enter new markets to spread risk

starter: Give two ways a market can be segmented.

teach.heading: Bismillah: growth with barakah
bullets: Growth is a goal, not a licence to cut corners
Seek success through lawful, fair means
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Recall the reported saying in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim that if buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their trade is blessed; if they conceal and lie, the blessing is lost. Set the theme for Theme 2: how a business can grow, and what it must consider on the way.

teach.heading: Why businesses grow
bullets: Economies of scale: lower unit costs
teach.note: Link back to Theme 1 aims. Ask: why would a successful single-site bakery want a second branch? Draw out profit, security and market share. Warn that bigger is not always better, which we will see with diseconomies.

teach.heading: Measuring growth
teach.note: Use the formula: percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100. Worked: revenue rises from 80,000 to 92,000 pounds. Change 12,000 / 80,000 = 0.15, so 15 percent growth.

teach.heading: Organic growth methods
bullets: Enter new markets, such as online
Open new branches funded by profits
teach.note: Explain organic = internal. Examples: a halal burger kiosk adds a delivery app and a new menu item. Ask: how is this different from buying a rival kiosk? (Using own resources and sales, not acquisition.)

teach.heading: Advantages and disadvantages
teach.note: Model a balanced judgement: organic growth is safer but slower, so rivals may take the market in the meantime. Remind pupils that Edexcel assess questions need a justified conclusion.

practice: Calculate the percentage growth if sales rise from 50,000 to 60,000 pounds.
Give two ways a small halal grocer could grow organically.
State two reasons why a business might want to grow.
independent: Explain two reasons why a successful restaurant might want to grow (4 marks style).
A business grows revenue from 120,000 to 138,000 pounds. Calculate percentage growth and comment on whether this is strong.
Write a paragraph assessing whether organic growth is the best way for a small business to expand.
exit: Define 'organic growth'.
State one disadvantage of organic growth.
lessons.homework: Choose a business you know and write six sentences explaining how it has grown organically.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: percentage change formula card with worked boxes. Stretch: discuss how growth might conflict with a business's ethical aims.

lessons.title: External growth: mergers and takeovers
objectives: Distinguish between a merger and a takeover
Evaluate the benefits and risks of external growth for a business

keywords.def: when two businesses agree to join together to form one business
when one business buys enough shares to gain control of another
growth by joining with or taking over another business
joining with a business at the same stage of production
joining with a business at a different stage of the supply chain

starter: Calculate percentage growth: revenue from 40,000 to 46,000 pounds.
Give one advantage of organic growth.

teach.heading: What is external growth?
bullets: Often needs a lot of money
Two main routes: merger or takeover
teach.note: Contrast with last lesson: organic = from within, external = joining with another firm. Ask pupils why a business might choose speed over control.

teach.heading: Mergers and takeovers
bullets: Merger: two firms agree to join
Takeover: one firm buys control of another
Takeovers can be friendly or hostile
teach.note: The Disney and Pixar example is real: Disney acquired Pixar in 2006. Keep other details out unless you have checked them. Misconception: merger and takeover are identical. In a merger both agree to form one company; in a takeover one buyer controls the other.

teach.heading: Types of integration
bullets: Backward vertical: bakery buys a flour mill
Forward vertical: bakery buys retail shops
Aims: more market share or control of supply
teach.note: Treat as an extension for stronger pupils. Draw a supply chain with flour mill, bakery, shop. Ask which type of integration gives control over costs and which gives more customers.

teach.heading: Benefits of external growth
bullets: Rapid increase in size and market share
Access to new markets, skills and brands
teach.note: Give a case: a halal sauce company takes over a rival that exports to the Middle East. It instantly gains new customers and export contacts. Discuss why this is quicker than building those contacts from scratch.

teach.heading: Risks and problems
bullets: High cost of buying the business
Job losses and loss of trust
The combined business may be hard to manage
teach.note: Add ethical considerations: staff must be treated fairly during redundancies; honesty with shareholders and workers matters. Ask pupils to give a final judgement on a case: is it better for a small firm to merge or to stay organic? Justify.

practice: Explain the difference between a merger and a takeover.
State one benefit and one risk of external growth.
A small cafe chain buys a coffee supplier. Is this horizontal or vertical integration? Explain.
independent: Explain two reasons why a company might take over a rival (4 marks style).
Case study: two halal food retailers merge and there are job losses. Analyse one possible effect on employees.
Write a paragraph evaluating whether external growth is better than organic growth for a medium-sized business.
exit: Define 'takeover'.
State one problem a business might face after merging.
lessons.homework: Research a real merger or takeover and write six sentences on why it happened and what the effects were.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: merger/takeover comparison table to complete. Stretch: evaluate how culture differences between firms could cause a merger to fail.

lessons.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
objectives: Describe types of economies of scale and calculate unit costs
Explain why businesses can suffer diseconomies of scale

keywords.def: falling average cost per unit as output rises
rising average cost per unit when a business becomes too big
total cost divided by the number of units produced
buying large quantities to get a lower price per item
workers or managers focusing on one type of task

starter: Give two reasons why a business might want to grow.
Calculate total cost: fixed 400 pounds and variable 600 pounds.

teach.heading: What are economies of scale?
bullets: Cost per unit falls as output rises
Not the same as total costs falling
teach.note: Misconception: total costs fall. Total costs rise as output rises; it is cost per unit that falls. Ask pupils why one loaf costs a bakery more to make when it bakes 10 loaves than when it bakes 1,000.

teach.heading: Types of economy of scale
bullets: Financial: cheaper loans for large firms
teach.note: Give a simple example of each. Purchasing: ordering 1,000 kg of flour for less per kilo. Technical: an industrial oven. Marketing economies can be added: one advert reaches many customers.

teach.heading: Worked example: calculating unit cost
bullets: Unit cost has fallen by 1.00 pound
teach.note: Work through the maths: 5,000 / 1,000 = 5; 20,000 / 5,000 = 4. Ask: what happens to profit per unit if the selling price is 6 pounds? (Profit per unit rises from 1 to 2 pounds.)

teach.heading: Diseconomies of scale
bullets: Communication problems in a large firm
teach.note: Use the idea of a school with 5,000 pupils: it would be harder for leaders to know everyone. Ask pupils to explain how poor communication might add costs. Show a U-shaped average cost curve verbally.

teach.heading: Managing growth wisely
bullets: Keep workers involved and fairly treated
Do not expand faster than you can manage
Keep quality and honesty at the centre
teach.note: Link to Islamic ethics: consultation (shura) and fair treatment of workers are part of good management. A large firm still owes honest dealing and fair wages.

practice: Calculate unit cost: 2,400 pounds for 600 units.
A firm buys flour in bulk and pays less per kilo. Identify the type of economy of scale.
Give two reasons why a very large business may have higher unit costs.
independent: Calculate the unit costs: 800 units for 4,000 pounds; 4,000 units for 14,000 pounds. Comment on the change.
Explain two economies of scale a growing halal food manufacturer could gain (4 marks style).
Write a paragraph assessing whether growth is always good for a business's unit costs.
exit: Define 'economies of scale'.
State one cause of diseconomies of scale.
lessons.homework: Write a short explanation, with a numerical example, of how bulk buying could lower the cost per unit for a school canteen.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: unit cost formula card and calculation boxes. Stretch: explain why fixed costs are important in economies of scale.

lessons.title: Financing growth: retained profit, loans and share capital
objectives: Describe the main sources of finance for business growth
Assess which source of finance suits a given situation, including the Islamic view of interest

keywords.def: profit kept in the business rather than paid to owners
money borrowed from a lender and repaid over time, usually with interest
the extra amount paid for borrowing money
money raised by selling shares in a company
interest or unjustified gain on a loan, which is forbidden in Islam

teach.heading: Why growth needs finance
bullets: New premises and equipment cost money
More stock and staff must be paid
Finance comes from inside or outside
teach.note: Link to growth methods. Ask pupils how a business with 5,000 pounds could open a new branch costing 40,000 pounds. Introduce internal and external sources.

teach.heading: Retained profit
bullets: Free of interest and no need to borrow
Only possible if the business is profitable
teach.note: Retained profit is the cheapest source but slow. Worked example: a business makes 30,000 pounds profit and retains 20,000 to fund a new oven. Ask why a new business may have little retained profit.

teach.heading: Loans
bullets: Borrow from a bank for a set period
Risk: repayments due even if sales fall
teach.note: Calculation: a 50,000 pound loan at 8 percent annual interest costs 4,000 pounds in interest a year (50,000 x 0.08). Ask: what if sales drop? Repayments still have to be made, so the risk stays with the borrower.

teach.heading: Share capital
bullets: Limited companies sell shares to investors
Owners must share profits and some control
teach.note: Distinguish sole traders (cannot sell shares) from limited companies. Shareholders receive dividends if profit is made. Misconception: shares must be repaid; they do not, but shareholders gain ownership.

teach.heading: Islamic note: interest and riba
bullets: Interest-based loans are riba in Islam
Qur'an 2:275: trade is lawful, riba is forbidden
Ask qualified scholars about specific contracts
teach.note: Present respectfully and as a note. Qur'an 2:275 says that Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba. Muslim business owners may prefer retained profit, investment from partners who share profit and loss (musharakah or mudarabah), or halal shares. Mention that the exam still expects knowledge of loans and interest; our faith position does not prevent us from understanding them. For specific contracts, advise pupils to consult a qualified scholar.

practice: Calculate annual interest on a 20,000 pound loan at 5 percent.
State one advantage and one disadvantage of retained profit.
Why can a sole trader not raise finance by selling shares?
independent: Explain two reasons why a growing company might use retained profit rather than a loan (4 marks style).
A halal restaurant chain wants 100,000 pounds to open three branches. Recommend a source of finance and justify your choice.
Write a paragraph assessing whether share capital is better than loans for financing growth.
exit: Define 'retained profit'.
State one drawback of using a loan to finance growth.
lessons.homework: Write six sentences comparing two sources of finance for a business wanting to open a second shop, including one halal-compatible alternative.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: comparison table with sentence starters. Stretch: evaluate the effect of interest on a start-up's profit.

lessons.title: Changing aims and objectives as a business grows
objectives: Explain why a business's aims and objectives change over time
Analyse how internal and external factors influence these changes

keywords.def: the long-term goals of a business
the state of demand, competition and the economy affecting a business
machines, systems and digital tools used to produce and sell
laws that businesses must follow
how well a business is doing against its targets

starter: Name two sources of finance for growth.
Calculate annual interest: 10,000 pounds at 6 percent.

teach.heading: Aims are not fixed
bullets: Mature aim: market share and reputation
Aims can also shift to social goals
teach.note: Recall Year 10 aims. Tell the story of a fictional business, Noor's Kitchen: year 1 survive, year 3 grow to two sites, year 6 become the best-known halal caterer. Ask why aims changed.

teach.heading: Market conditions and competition
bullets: Business may aim to cut costs or diversify
teach.note: Give an example: a recession means customers spend less. A business may change its objective from growth to cost control. Ask pupils to justify the change.

teach.heading: Technology and legislation
bullets: New laws, such as minimum wage rises, raise costs
Health and safety rules change operations
teach.note: Keep examples general and accurate. Ask pupils how an online ordering system might change an objective from local to national sales. Add that obeying the law and keeping promises is part of trustworthy trade.

teach.heading: Performance and owners' choices
bullets: Success may lead to bigger targets
Poor results may switch aims back to survival
teach.note: Link aims with the stage of a business. Worked example of market share: Noor's Kitchen has sales of 60,000 pounds in a market of 1,200,000 pounds. Market share = 60,000 / 1,200,000 x 100 = 5 percent. Objective: raise to 8 percent within two years.

teach.heading: Evaluating change
teach.note: Model an evaluation: changing aims can help a business adapt, but constant change may confuse staff and customers. Ask for a justified view on a case.

practice: Give one reason why a start-up's aim of survival might later change to growth.
Calculate market share: sales 30,000 pounds in a market of 600,000 pounds.
State two external factors that could change a business's objectives.
independent: Explain two reasons why a business might change its objectives from growth to survival (4 marks style).
Case study: a halal supermarket faces a new rival and rising costs. Analyse how its objectives might change.
Write a paragraph assessing the most important factor in changing aims and objectives.
exit: State one reason why aims change over time.
Calculate market share: 5,000 pounds sales in a 100,000 pound market.
lessons.homework: Choose a business and write six sentences on how its aims might differ in year 1 and year 10.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline cards for Noor's Kitchen. Stretch: assess whether external or internal factors matter most.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Globalisation, ethics and the environment
lessons.title: Business and globalisation: trading across borders
objectives: Define globalisation, imports, exports and multinationals
Evaluate the opportunities and challenges of selling and producing abroad

keywords.def: the growing connection between businesses and economies across the world
a good or service bought from another country
a good or service sold to another country
a business that operates in more than one country
customers in other countries who buy a business's products

starter: State one reason why aims change.

teach.heading: What is globalisation?
bullets: Goods, money and ideas move easily
Transport and the internet speed it up
teach.note: Ask pupils to check the labels of their clothes or phones: where were they made? Introduce the idea that even a small shop can buy from or sell to other countries. Qur'an 49:13 says that Allah made people into nations and tribes so that they may know one another; use it to open discussion of respect between cultures.

teach.heading: Imports and exports
bullets: Importers can access cheaper or unique goods
teach.note: Misconception: imports are always cheaper or poorer quality. Give example: a UK dates retailer imports dates grown in warmer countries. Ask who benefits.

teach.heading: Why sell abroad?
bullets: Spread risk if home sales fall
teach.note: Work through a case: a UK modest-fashion brand finds demand in other countries through online sales. Ask what research it needs first. Link to market research from Year 10.

teach.heading: Multinational businesses
bullets: Benefit from lower costs and large markets
Local businesses may struggle to compete
Can bring jobs but may move them away
teach.note: Discuss advantages and disadvantages for both the multinational and the host country. Provide balance: multinationals can create jobs and investment, but may squeeze local firms or pay low wages.

teach.heading: Challenges of trading abroad
teach.note: Practical example: product labelling and halal certification differ by country. Ask how a business can adapt (translate packaging, understand local tastes). Stress honest labelling.

practice: Define 'export' and give one example.
State two benefits to a UK firm of selling its products abroad.
Explain one problem a small business might face when selling in another country.
independent: Explain two benefits to a business of becoming a multinational (4 marks style).
Case study: a UK halal food firm starts exporting. Analyse two issues it must consider.
Write a paragraph assessing whether globalisation helps or harms small local businesses.
exit: Define 'globalisation'.
State one advantage of exporting.
lessons.homework: Look at five items in your home and write down where each was made; explain two benefits of global trade to you as a customer.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: world map matching of imports/exports with labels. Stretch: evaluate the effect of globalisation on a local halal butcher.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Globalisation, ethics and the environment
lessons.title: Trade barriers, e-commerce and changing location
objectives: Describe tariffs, quotas and trade blocs and explain their effects on business
Assess how e-commerce and changing location affect businesses

keywords.def: a tax placed on imported goods, making them more expensive
a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
a group of countries that agree to trade freely with each other
buying and selling goods and services over the internet
moving production or services to another country, often to cut costs

starter: Give one benefit of selling abroad.

teach.heading: Barriers to trade
bullets: Governments restrict imports to protect jobs
Both can raise prices for customers
teach.note: Explain why governments use barriers: protect home industries and jobs. Ask pupils who gains and who loses.

teach.heading: Worked example: a tariff
bullets: Importer may raise prices or cut profit
teach.note: Calculation: 10 percent of 20,000 = 2,000; 20,000 + 2,000 = 22,000. Ask pupils what options the importer has: pass on the cost, accept lower profit, or find a different supplier.

teach.heading: Trade blocs
bullets: Easier for firms to export within the bloc
teach.note: Define a trade bloc with the EU as an example. Ask how membership or leaving a trade bloc could affect the cost of importing for a UK retailer. Keep to general effects.

teach.heading: E-commerce
bullets: Lower costs than renting many shops
teach.note: Link to market research and segmentation. Ask: how can a small online modest-fashion shop reach the world? What are the delivery and returns challenges? Remind pupils of honesty in descriptions: the item should match what is shown.

teach.heading: Changing location of production
bullets: Risks: poor quality control and bad publicity
Fair pay and conditions still matter
teach.note: Evaluate: offshoring may cut costs but harms home workers and could risk exploitation. Link forward to ethics in the next lesson. Ask for a justified decision on a case.

practice: Calculate the cost after a 15 percent tariff on 8,000 pounds of imports.
Explain the difference between a tariff and a quota.
State two advantages of e-commerce for a small retailer.
independent: Explain two effects of a tariff on a UK importer (4 marks style).
Case study: a clothing firm moves production abroad to cut costs. Analyse one benefit and one risk.
Write a paragraph assessing whether e-commerce is more important than trade blocs for helping a small business trade abroad.
exit: Define 'tariff'.
Give one advantage of e-commerce.
lessons.homework: Research one product you use that is traded across borders and write six sentences on how tariffs or e-commerce might affect its price or availability.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: tariff calculation frame and vocabulary matching. Stretch: evaluate whether free trade benefits all countries equally.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Globalisation, ethics and the environment
lessons.title: Ethics, the environment and business decisions
objectives: Explain ethical and environmental issues that affect business decisions
Evaluate the trade-off between profit and acting ethically and sustainably

keywords.def: moral principles about what is right and wrong in business decisions
meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
a group that tries to influence businesses or government on an issue
giving up one benefit to gain another
what customers and the public think of a business

starter: Calculate a 10 percent tariff on 5,000 pounds of imports.
State one way e-commerce helps small businesses.

teach.heading: Ethics in business
bullets: Fair pay and safe working conditions
No exploitation of workers or suppliers
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Qur'an 83:1-3 condemns those who cheat when measuring for others, and Qur'an 6:152 commands giving full measure and weight with justice. A reported saying in Jami at-Tirmidhi states that the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. Ask: what does it mean to run a business with amanah (trust)?

teach.heading: Environmental impact
teach.note: Link to stewardship: Qur'an 2:30 describes human beings as khalifah on earth, and 7:31 says do not waste. Ask pupils to list ways a takeaway could reduce waste (recyclable packaging, surplus food donation).

teach.heading: Costs and benefits of acting ethically
bullets: Costs: higher production costs and prices
Benefits: loyal customers and good reputation
teach.note: Work through a case: a halal chicken supplier decides to improve welfare standards and pays farmers more. Costs per pack rise by 20p, but more customers choose it. Ask whether the trade-off is worthwhile.

teach.heading: Pressure groups and consumers
bullets: Pressure groups campaign and raise awareness
Customers can boycott or switch brands
teach.note: Explain that pressure groups can damage reputation; businesses may respond by changing practices. Misconception: ethics only matter to big firms. Small firms also depend on trust.

teach.heading: Making a balanced decision
bullets: Weigh profit against ethics and the planet
Consider the short and long term
teach.note: Teach a 9-mark judgement structure: points for and against, link to context, then a justified conclusion. Practise with: Should a clothing firm use more expensive, ethically sourced cotton?

practice: Give two examples of unethical business behaviour.
State two ways a business can reduce its environmental impact.
Explain one possible benefit to a business of having a good reputation.
independent: Explain two possible costs to a business of acting ethically (4 marks style).
Case study: a clothing company uses cheaper suppliers with poor working conditions. Analyse two possible consequences for the company.
Write a paragraph evaluating whether profit or ethics should come first when making business decisions. Reach a justified conclusion.
exit: Define 'sustainability'.
Give one reason why acting ethically can help a business.
lessons.homework: Choose a well-known business and write a short evaluation of its ethical or environmental practices, using at least two pieces of evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: costs/benefits table with sentence starters. Stretch: compare ethical decision-making for a small firm and a multinational.

lessons.title: Training: induction, on-the-job and off-the-job
lessons.bigQuestion: Is training a cost or an investment?
objectives: Explain why training matters to the business and to workers
Describe induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training
Evaluate benefits and limitations, including health and safety compliance
successCriteria: All: name three types of training and one benefit
Most: compare on-the-job and off-the-job training
Some: justify a training method for a given worker and cost
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: careers and workplace safety; Maths: cost and payback
lessons.smsc: Moral: valuing workers' growth and keeping them safe, a duty of care

keywords.def: an introduction to the business for a new employee
learning while doing the job, supported by a colleague
learning away from the workplace, such as a college course
protecting people from harm at work
the percentage of staff leaving a business in a year

starter: Name one benefit of internal recruitment.
State one legal control on recruitment.

teach.heading: Why train?
bullets: Keeps staff motivated so fewer leave
Helps the business meet safety rules
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Cedar Bakery Ltd with 20 staff. A trained baker wastes fewer ingredients. Ask: what benefits does the worker gain? New skills, promotion chances, confidence. Link to Islamic teaching on seeking beneficial knowledge as a general encouragement to learn; let the teacher expand without quotations.

teach.heading: Three types
teach.note: Table. Induction: first days, tour, safety rules, introductions. On-the-job: watching Hamza the senior baker. Off-the-job: day-release food hygiene course. Ask pupils which type new staff need first. Misconception: induction is not full training for the job; it is an orientation.

head: Type
What happens
Benefit
Limitation
rows: Learning at work from a colleague

teach.heading: Health and safety
bullets: Fewer accidents mean less lost time and lower costs
teach.note: Link to food hygiene in the bakery: a trained worker knows about storing food at the right temperature. Ask about the cost of an accident: sick pay, compensation, lost production, damaged reputation. Emphasise that protecting workers from harm is part of fair treatment.

teach.heading: Worked example: is training worth it?
teach.note: Model a simple cost-benefit. Ask what else matters (will the worker stay? quality?). Remind pupils to include the lost output while away from work in cost.

model.problem: Cedar Bakery sends 4 staff on a food hygiene course costing 150 pounds each. Each is away for one day and daily output lost is worth 80 pounds each. The firm expects to save 1,200 pounds a year in wasted food. What is the first-year net benefit?
model.answer: Net benefit of 280 pounds in year one

teach.heading: Check: training type
teach.note: Answer C. Learning at the same workplace from a colleague is on-the-job. A is orientation only.

check.q: A new apprentice learns to decorate cakes by working beside a senior baker. Which type is this?
check.why: Learning while doing the job at work is on-the-job training.

teach.heading: Limitations of training
bullets: Trained staff may leave for better pay
Benefits may take time to appear
Not all staff will want to learn
teach.note: Discuss the risk of a trained worker leaving for a rival. How can the business reduce it? Better pay, promotion, contract terms. Evaluate: overall training usually pays off if the business keeps staff and uses the skills.

practice: Calculate the cost of sending 6 staff on a 200 pounds course with lost output of 90 pounds each.
State two benefits of induction.
Explain one disadvantage of off-the-job training.
independent: Core: Match five staff (new starter, cashier, chef needing new skills) to a suitable training type.
Extend: Explain how training can help a business meet health and safety rules.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A firm of 10 staff can run on-the-job training at no cost or pay 3,000 pounds for a college course. Which should it choose?
exit: Define induction.
Give two benefits of training to workers.
Big question: is training a cost or an investment? One sentence.
lessons.homework: Write a short induction checklist for a new member of staff at a business of your choice.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a three-column sort for types. EAL: use pictures for induction. Stretch: consider how staff turnover alters the value of training.

lessons.title: Motivation: theories, pay and non-financial rewards
lessons.bigQuestion: Is money the only reason people work hard?
objectives: Explain why motivation matters
Describe the theories of Taylor, Maslow and Herzberg
Describe financial and non-financial methods and judge which suits a business
successCriteria: All: define motivation and name three methods
Most: explain each theory in one sentence and give a method for each
Some: justify the best motivation method for a given group
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: wellbeing at work; Islamic Studies: fair pay and treatment of workers (enrichment)
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair, prompt pay and dignity at work; the teacher may expand on Islamic teaching about treatment of workers without quotation here

keywords.def: the desire to work hard and do a good job
scientific management: pay is the main motivator
hierarchy of needs: people are motivated by unmet needs
two factors: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, motivators create satisfaction
giving workers more challenging and rewarding tasks
pay linked to the value of sales made
extra rewards such as a company car or staff discount

starter: Why might a trained worker leave?

teach.heading: Why motivation matters
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Pinnacle Call Centre where staff turnover is 40 per cent a year. Cost of recruiting each replacement is 1,500 pounds. Calculate: with 100 staff, 40 leave at 1,500 each = 60,000 pounds a year. Ask what the firm could do. Draw out that motivation is partly about money and partly about the work itself.

teach.heading: Three theories
teach.note: Table. Taylor: workers lazy, pay by output. Maslow: five levels from physical needs to self-actualisation; a worker who fears for their job is not helped by a trophy. Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, security) stop dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, responsibility, recognition) give real motivation. Ask pupils to place a bonus and a promotion.

head: Theorist
Main idea
Business action
rows: Needs form a ladder: basic, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation

teach.heading: Financial methods
bullets: Fringe benefits: perks like staff discount
teach.note: Give examples from Pinnacle. A seller earns 5 per cent commission on 40,000 pounds sales: 2,000 pounds. Discuss limits: commission can encourage pressure selling and dishonesty, so honesty must be rewarded too. Ask: which suits a team? Bonuses that depend on teamwork. Pay should also be fair and on time; teachers may expand on Islamic teaching on fair pay.

teach.heading: Worked example: commission
teach.note: Show the pay calculation. Ask whether the worker would be motivated if sales fell. Link to risk and Taylor's view.

model.problem: Samira earns a basic wage of 1,600 pounds a month plus 4% commission on sales. She sells 35,000 pounds of goods this month. Calculate her total pay.

teach.heading: Non-financial methods
bullets: Job enrichment: more challenge and responsibility
Autonomy: freedom to decide how to work
teach.note: Link each to Herzberg motivators. A worker who handles customer complaints alone has autonomy. Discuss limitations: enrichment needs training and time; not every worker wants more responsibility. Ask pupils to decide which would help at Pinnacle.

teach.heading: Check: theory
teach.note: Answer B. Herzberg's motivators include recognition. Taylor focuses on pay.

check.q: A manager gives staff more responsibility and public praise for achievements. Which theory best supports this?
check.why: Responsibility, achievement and recognition are Herzberg motivators. Taylor is about money.

teach.heading: Choosing a method
bullets: Use the nature of the work and the workers
teach.note: Practise evaluation: for a seasonal worker, a bonus may motivate more; for a long-term professional, autonomy may. Remind the class that a reasoned conclusion that refers to the business earns the higher marks.

practice: A worker earns 1,200 pounds plus 6% commission on 25,000 pounds sales. Calculate the total.
Give one financial and one non-financial method of motivation.
Explain one limitation of paying only by commission.
independent: Core: Match six actions (pay rise, safe working conditions, team events) to Maslow's levels.
Extend: Explain how Herzberg's theory differs from Taylor's.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Pinnacle can offer a 5% pay rise costing 90,000 pounds or job enrichment and training costing 40,000 pounds to cut turnover. Which is better?
exit: Define motivation.
Name one hygiene factor and one motivator.
Big question: is money the only reason people work hard? One reason for and one against.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about what keeps them motivated at work and link two answers to a theory.
lessons.send: SEND: use a ladder diagram for Maslow. EAL: pre-teach commission, bonus. Stretch: criticise one theory.

lessons.title: Organisation structure: hierarchy, span of control and functional areas
lessons.bigQuestion: Who should make the decisions in a business?
objectives: Compare hierarchical and flat structures and centralised and decentralised decisions
Explain span of control, chain of command and delegation
Describe the functions of HR, finance, marketing and production
successCriteria: All: define span of control and chain of command
Most: compare tall and flat structures
Some: judge whether a business should centralise decisions
lessons.smsc: Moral: trust, responsibility and accountability (amanah) when authority is delegated

keywords.def: levels of authority from top to bottom in a business
the line along which orders are passed down
the number of workers directly managed by one manager
passing authority and tasks to someone lower down
decisions made by senior managers at the top
decisions made by staff at lower levels

starter: Name one financial and one non-financial motivation method.

teach.heading: Hierarchy and chain of command
bullets: Orders pass down the chain of command
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Oasis Water Ltd with 60 staff. Draw its chart: managing director, three managers, six supervisors, 50 workers. Ask: how many levels? Four. Discuss messages passing down and slowed communication in a tall structure. Link to the communication lesson.

teach.heading: Span of control
teach.note: Model the calculation. A narrow span means tight supervision; a wide span means freedom but pressure on the manager. Ask whether more supervision always equals better performance. Draw out that it depends on training and trust. Note that in a flat structure the span is wider.

model.problem: At Oasis Water, a supervisor manages 8 workers directly. The firm has 48 workers on the factory floor. How many supervisors are needed, and what is the span of control?
steps: Span of control = number of staff directly managed
model.answer: Span of control is 8 and 6 supervisors are needed

teach.heading: Flat and tall; centralised and decentralised
teach.note: Compare. Flat: faster communication, cheaper, empowers workers; tall: clear promotion path, close supervision, but slower and costly. Centralised: consistent decisions, but slow and unaware of local needs. Decentralised: faster and motivating, but risk of inconsistent decisions. Ask pupils which suits a multinational.

teach.heading: Delegation
bullets: Manager passes tasks and authority down
Risk: task done badly; manager still accountable
teach.note: Ask: what must be given with the task? Authority and trust. Link to amanah: someone given responsibility should carry it honestly; teacher may expand. Misconception: delegation is not dumping work; support and clear instructions are needed.

teach.heading: Functional areas
bullets: Production: making goods or delivering services
teach.note: Use a quick match: pupils decide which department handles each of eight tasks (for example paying suppliers: finance; running a promotion: marketing). Note departments must co-operate: marketing's promise must be possible for production.

teach.heading: Check: structure
teach.note: Answer C. Wide span with few levels is a flat structure. A is the opposite.

check.q: A firm has three layers, and each manager supervises 15 staff. Which structure does it show?
check.why: Few layers and many staff per manager is a flat structure with a wide span.

practice: A manager has 36 staff and a span of control of 6 per supervisor. How many supervisors are needed?
Name the four functional areas.
Explain one benefit of delegation.
independent: Core: Draw an organisation chart for a fictional school bus company with 15 staff and label the chain of command.
Extend: Explain two effects of a tall structure on communication.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A fast-growing firm with 80 staff can make all decisions centrally or let branch managers decide. Which should it choose?
exit: Define span of control.
State one benefit and one drawback of a flat structure.
Big question: who should make the decisions? Give a reason.
lessons.homework: Draw the structure of your school or masjid committee and identify the chain of command.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a partially completed organisation chart. EAL: pre-teach hierarchy, delegate. Stretch: relate structures to business growth.

lessons.title: Sources of finance: how does a business pay for what it needs?
lessons.bigQuestion: If a business needs 50,000 pounds, where can it get it?
objectives: Distinguish short-term and long-term finance and start-up and expansion needs
Describe internal and external sources of finance
Choose suitable finance for a given business, including an Islamic-finance-aware note
successCriteria: All: name three internal and three external sources
Most: say which source suits a short-term or a long-term need
Some: justify the best source of finance for a given business
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and interest; Islamic Studies: lawful trade and riba (enrichment)
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest borrowing and repaying; many Muslims avoid interest-based finance as a widely held position, so the teacher may expand on halal alternatives

keywords.def: borrowing from a bank account beyond the balance, usually short term
profit kept in the business rather than paid out
money owed to suppliers for goods bought on credit
a sum borrowed and repaid with interest over a period
money raised by selling shares
selling shares to the public for the first time
money invested by specialist investors in risky businesses
raising small sums from many people, usually online

starter: Which ownership form can sell shares to the public?

teach.heading: Why businesses need finance
bullets: Short-term: pay bills until customers pay
Long-term: buy assets that last years
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Falcon Print Shop. Starting costs: 12,000 for a printer, 3,000 for first stock. Ask: what is the difference between money needed for months and for years? Match finance period to need: do not use a short-term overdraft to buy a building.

teach.heading: Internal sources
bullets: Personal savings: no interest but owner's risk
Retained profit: cheap and flexible, but only for established firms
Selling assets: quick cash but loses something useful
teach.note: Ask which a new business can use (savings). Retained profit needs a profitable business. Discuss selling a spare delivery van: cash but fewer assets. Internal sources do not need to be repaid or involve interest payments.

teach.heading: External sources
teach.note: Table. Link each to the business type. A sole trader cannot sell shares. Flotation is only for a plc. Venture capital investors expect a share and a high return. Note: loans and overdrafts usually carry interest. A widely held view among Muslims is that interest-based finance is to be avoided; many Islamic finance products are structured differently, but do not give rulings. The teacher may expand with local scholarly advice.

head: Source
Term
Cost or drawback
Suits
rows: Investors want a share and control

teach.heading: Worked example: cost of a loan
teach.note: Walk through simple interest. Compare to share capital: no interest, but sharing profit. Discuss how a person who avoids interest might look at partnership or share capital instead; do not state rulings.

model.problem: Falcon Print borrows 20,000 pounds at 8% a year for 3 years, repaying the 20,000 at the end and paying interest each year. Calculate the total interest.
model.answer: Total interest 4,800 pounds; total repaid 24,800 pounds

teach.heading: Check: match source to need
teach.note: Answer D. A temporary gap in cash is best covered short term with an overdraft. A is long-term finance.

check.q: Falcon Print needs 4,000 pounds for three weeks to cover wages until a customer pays. Which is most suitable?
check.why: An overdraft is flexible short-term finance. Flotation and share capital are long-term sources.

teach.heading: Choosing the best source
bullets: Cost: interest or lost profit share
Risk: can they repay if sales fall?
teach.note: Practice with scenarios: a new market stall with 2,000 pounds need; a plc buying a factory worth 5 million; an inventor with a risky idea. Always justify with context. Remind pupils that in the exam context information in the case often points to the answer.

practice: Falcon borrows 15,000 pounds at 6% a year for 2 years. Calculate total interest.
State two internal sources of finance.
Explain one drawback of selling shares.
independent: Core: Match six situations to the best source of finance.
Extend: Explain why retained profit is not available to a new business.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A new bakery needs 30,000 pounds. The owner has 5,000 of savings. Compare a bank loan, crowdfunding and a partner, and recommend one.
exit: Define retained profit.
Name one short-term and one long-term source.
Big question: where can 50,000 pounds come from? List two.
lessons.homework: Ask an adult how they paid for something big and classify the source as internal or external.
lessons.send: SEND: use cards for matching. EAL: use pictures for loan, overdraft. Stretch: compare finance for a plc and a sole trader.

lessons.title: Cash flow forecasting: why cash matters more than profit
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a profitable business run out of cash?
objectives: Explain why cash is needed and why shortages risk insolvency
Distinguish cash from profit
Calculate net cash flow and opening and closing balances and interpret a forecast
successCriteria: All: define cash inflow, outflow and net cash flow
Most: complete a cash flow forecast table
Some: interpret a forecast and recommend how to fix a shortage
lessons.smsc: Moral: paying suppliers and workers on time is a matter of honesty and trust

keywords.def: the movement of money into and out of a business
money received by the business
money paid out by the business
inflows minus outflows in a period
cash at the start of a period
cash at the end of a period; it becomes next month's opening balance
being unable to pay debts when they are due

starter: Name one internal source of finance.
State one drawback of an overdraft.

teach.heading: Cash is not profit
bullets: Profit: revenue minus costs over a period
A firm can be profitable but short of cash
Customers may pay late; suppliers want paying now
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Harbour Fish Ltd. It sells 60,000 pounds of fish on credit in March, but customers pay in May. In March it must pay wages and suppliers. It shows a profit, but the bank balance is empty. Ask: could it close? Introduce insolvency. Misconception: more sales always mean more cash; late payment can cause shortages.

teach.heading: The forecast table
teach.note: Present the structure. Opening balance + net cash flow = closing balance, and closing balance becomes next month's opening. A negative closing balance means the firm needs an overdraft or other finance. Stress inflows: sales, loans; outflows: wages, rent, materials. Ask which line is the closing balance for February.

teach.heading: Worked example: completing a forecast
teach.note: Model carefully with negative numbers. Point out March's closing balance equals April's opening. Ask what the firm should do in the second month: a cash shortage even in a profitable year.

model.problem: Harbour Fish opens April with 4,000 pounds. April inflows 10,000, outflows 12,500. May inflows 11,000, outflows 9,000. Find the closing balances.
model.answer: April closing 1,500 pounds; May closing 3,500 pounds

teach.heading: Check: balances
teach.note: Answer C. Opening 2,500 + inflows 4,000 - outflows 5,500 = 1,000. A ignores outflows.

check.q: A business has an opening balance of 2,500 pounds, inflows of 4,000 and outflows of 5,500. What is the closing balance?
check.why: 2,500 + 4,000 - 5,500 = 1,000. Adding the outflow is the usual slip.

teach.heading: Solving cash problems
bullets: Ask suppliers for longer to pay
teach.note: Link to sources of finance. Evaluate: asking customers to pay sooner may annoy them; delaying supplier payments may harm relationships and trust. Remind pupils that paying on time is an honest practice. Insolvency means the firm cannot pay debts when due, even if its assets are worth more.

practice: Opening 1,200, inflows 5,000, outflows 6,800. Calculate the closing balance.
Explain the difference between cash and profit.
State two ways to improve a negative cash flow.
independent: Core: Complete a four-month cash flow forecast for a fictional ice-cream van.
Extend: Explain why a growing business can run out of cash.
Stretch: Analyse (6 marks): Harbour Fish's forecast shows negative balances in two months. Analyse two ways to respond and the effect of each.
exit: Define net cash flow.
What does a negative closing balance show?
Big question: how can a profitable business run out of cash? One sentence.
lessons.homework: Draw a six-line cash forecast for pocket money, with inflows, outflows and closing balances for four weeks.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-labelled table with formula prompts. EAL: use pictures of in and out for inflow and outflow. Stretch: consider seasonal businesses.

lessons.title: Costs, revenue and break-even
lessons.bigQuestion: How many sales does a business need before it stops losing money?
objectives: Define revenue, fixed costs, variable costs, total costs, profit and loss
Calculate break-even output and margin of safety
Interpret a break-even chart, the effect of changes in price or cost and the limitations of the method
successCriteria: All: calculate revenue, total cost and profit
Most: calculate break-even output by formula
Some: interpret a chart and evaluate the limits of break-even analysis
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: linear graphs and substitution; Computing: spreadsheets
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest pricing and realistic planning; avoiding unrealistic promises to investors

keywords.def: a cost that does not change with output, such as rent
a cost that changes with output, such as materials
fixed costs plus variable costs
price multiplied by quantity sold
the output at which total revenue equals total cost
selling price minus variable cost per unit
actual or planned output minus break-even output

starter: Calculate closing balance: opening 800, inflows 3,000, outflows 3,500.
Name one cause of a cash shortage.

teach.heading: Revenue and costs
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Zenith Candles, selling candles at 12 pounds each. Fixed cost 14,000 a year; variable cost 5 pounds per candle. Ask pupils: if it sells 1,000 candles, what is revenue (12,000), total cost (14,000+5,000=19,000), profit (-7,000)? Misconception: variable cost per unit stays the same, but total variable cost rises with output.

teach.heading: The break-even formula
teach.note: Introduce contribution per unit: price minus variable cost, which pays towards fixed costs. Break-even output = fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. Show Zenith: 12 - 5 = 7; 14,000 divided by 7 = 2,000 candles. Check by revenue 24,000 against total cost 14,000 + 10,000 = 24,000. Pupils should always check the answer this way.

model.problem: Zenith Candles: price 12 pounds, variable cost 5 pounds, fixed costs 14,000 pounds. Calculate break-even output and the margin of safety if it plans to sell 2,600 candles.
model.answer: Break-even 2,000 candles; margin of safety 600 candles

teach.heading: The break-even chart
teach.note: Describe: output on the horizontal axis, money on the vertical. Fixed costs are a horizontal line, total costs start at fixed costs and rise, revenue starts at zero and rises more steeply. They cross at break-even. Below it: loss; above: profit. Use the table to plot points. Ask pupils to read the chart at 3,000 candles: profit of 7,000.

teach.heading: Check: break-even
teach.note: Answer A. 9,000 / (15 - 6) = 1,000. Distractor C divides by price only.

check.q: A firm has fixed costs of 9,000 pounds, a price of 15 pounds and variable cost of 6 pounds per unit. What is break-even output?
check.why: Contribution is 9; 9,000 divided by 9 = 1,000. Dividing by the price (600) is the common error.

teach.heading: What happens when things change?
bullets: Higher price: lower break-even, if sales hold
Margin of safety shows the cushion
teach.note: Use Zenith. Raise the price to 13: contribution 8, break-even 1,750. Ask what the risk is: fewer customers. Raise rent by 2,000 a year: break-even 16,000 divided by 7 about 2,286. Make pupils compute one change themselves.

teach.heading: Limitations
bullets: Assumes constant price and variable cost per unit
Costs and prices change in real life
teach.note: Evaluation point for the 20-mark question. Break-even is a planning aid: useful for loans and pricing, but only as reliable as the data. Honesty in planning: an owner should present realistic figures to lenders or investors; the teacher may expand with Islamic ethics on honest dealing.

practice: Fixed costs 18,000, price 20, variable cost 8. Calculate break-even output.
Zenith sells 3,400 candles. Using break-even 2,000, calculate margin of safety.
Explain one limitation of break-even analysis.
independent: Core: Complete a break-even table for a fictional juice stall and read the break-even point.
Extend: Calculate the new break-even after a price rise from 12 to 14 pounds with variable cost 5 pounds and fixed costs 14,000.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Zenith could raise its price to 13 pounds or cut variable costs by buying cheaper wax at 4 pounds a candle. Which gives the lower break-even and which is riskier?
exit: State the break-even formula.
Define margin of safety.
Big question: how many sales before it stops losing money? Answer using a number from today.
lessons.homework: Create break-even calculations for a small business idea with your own fixed and variable costs.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a formula card and a partly filled table. EAL: pre-teach contribution. Stretch: use a spreadsheet to draw the chart.

lessons.title: Financial documents: reading the income statement and the statement of financial position
lessons.bigQuestion: What can two pages of numbers tell us about a business?
objectives: Interpret the statement of comprehensive income: sales, cost of sales, gross profit, expenses, operating profit
Interpret the statement of financial position: current and non-current assets and liabilities, capital employed
Explain why candidates interpret but do not construct them
successCriteria: All: identify gross profit and operating profit in a table
Most: classify items as current or non-current assets or liabilities
Some: calculate capital employed and comment on a document
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and arithmetic with large numbers
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest accounting and transparency in reporting; trust with investors and the tax authority

keywords.def: the direct cost of producing the goods sold
sales minus cost of sales
gross profit minus expenses
an asset kept for more than a year, such as machinery
an asset likely to become cash within a year, such as inventory or receivables
a debt due within a year
long-term funds in the business: equity plus non-current liabilities
goods held for sale or materials held for production

starter: Give one limitation of break-even analysis.

teach.heading: Why financial documents?
bullets: Show how a business has performed
Show what it owns and owes
Used by owners, banks, investors, tax authorities
International terms: inventory, statement of financial position
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Meridian Retail Ltd. Say that in the exam pupils read and interpret these statements but do not have to build them. Ask: who would want to read them and why? A bank deciding on a loan. Honest accounts are essential to trust; the teacher may expand on honesty in dealing.

teach.heading: The statement of comprehensive income
teach.note: Show the table and read down. Sales minus cost of sales gives gross profit; minus expenses gives operating profit. Ask which line shows how well products earn (gross profit) and which line shows overall trading success (operating profit). Misconception: profit is not the same as cash; the statement is a measure over a period.

head: Meridian Retail Ltd, year to 31 Dec
Pounds

teach.heading: The statement of financial position
teach.note: A snapshot on one date. Left side: assets; right: liabilities and equity. Non-current assets (shop fittings), current assets (inventory, receivables, cash). Current liabilities within a year, non-current liabilities longer term. Capital employed = total assets minus current liabilities = 340,000. Ask pupils to check it against equity + non-current liabilities = 240,000 + 100,000.

teach.heading: Worked example: capital employed
teach.note: Model both routes. Make sure pupils know that both must agree. Emphasise that capital employed is the long-term funding that the business uses to earn its profit.

model.problem: Using Meridian's figures, calculate capital employed in two ways.

teach.heading: Check: classify
teach.note: Answer C. Inventory is a current asset. Machinery is non-current; a five-year loan is a non-current liability.

check.q: Which item is a current asset?
check.why: Inventory should be turned into cash within a year, so it is a current asset. The van and fittings are non-current assets; the loan is a liability.

teach.heading: Reading with care
bullets: Compare with last year, not one year alone
Look at trends in sales and costs
Remember limits: past data, no non-financial information
teach.note: Show last year: sales 700,000, gross profit 266,000, operating profit 84,000. Ask what has changed: sales up, operating profit down. Pupils suggest causes: higher costs. Next lesson turns this into ratios. Remind them that exam questions give the layout; they should locate the figures and use them in context.

practice: Sales 500,000, cost of sales 300,000, expenses 120,000. Calculate gross profit and operating profit.
State two non-current assets for a restaurant.
Explain why a bank may study a business's statements.
independent: Core: Using a given statement, label each item as current or non-current and as an asset or a liability.
Extend: Calculate capital employed for a fictional business with total assets 520,000 and current liabilities 130,000.
Stretch: Analyse (6 marks): Meridian's sales rose by 14% but operating profit fell. Analyse two possible causes using the figures.
exit: Define gross profit.
Name one current liability.
Big question: what can two pages of numbers tell us? One thing.
lessons.homework: Choose a business you know and list what you would expect to see under non-current and current assets.
lessons.send: SEND: give coloured highlighting for sections of the statement. EAL: use glossary for inventory, receivables. Stretch: link to cash flow and profit differences.

lessons.title: Accounts analysis: profit margins, markup, ROCE and liquidity ratios
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know whether a business is doing well?
objectives: Calculate gross and operating profit margin, markup, ROCE, current ratio and acid test ratio
Judge liquidity and compare over time or with competitors
Use financial documents to assess performance and inform decisions
successCriteria: All: calculate gross profit margin
Most: calculate and interpret all six ratios
Some: evaluate performance using ratios and make a decision
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest interpretation; not hiding poor results or exaggerating good ones

keywords.def: gross profit as a percentage of sales
operating profit as a percentage of sales
profit as a percentage of cost
return on capital employed: operating profit as a percentage of capital employed
current assets divided by current liabilities
current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities
the ability to pay short-term debts

starter: State the formula for gross profit.

teach.heading: Profitability ratios
teach.note: Introduce the formulae (they are provided in the exam but pupils should know how to use them). Then use Meridian: sales 800,000, gross profit 320,000 gives 40%; operating profit 80,000 gives 10%. Last year: gross 38% and operating 12%. Ask: gross margin has improved but operating margin has fallen. Why? Higher expenses. Misconception: percentages are calculated from sales, not from cost.

teach.heading: Worked example: ROCE
teach.note: Walk through slowly. Ask what ROCE means: for each 100 pounds of long-term finance, about 23.5 pounds of operating profit. Compare with the interest rate on a loan or a saving account. A higher ROCE is better, and should be compared with last year or a rival.

model.problem: Zahid's Garden Centre has operating profit of 54,000 pounds and capital employed of 300,000 pounds. Last year ROCE was 15%. Calculate this year's ROCE and comment.
steps: ROCE = operating profit divided by capital employed x 100
model.answer: ROCE 18%, up 3 percentage points: improved performance

teach.heading: Liquidity ratios
teach.note: Explain current ratio and acid test with Meridian: current assets 120,000, current liabilities 80,000: current ratio 1.5; acid test = (120,000 - 60,000) / 80,000 = 0.75. A rule of thumb often used is about 1.5 to 2 for the current ratio and about 1 for the acid test, but it varies by industry, so teach caution. A low acid test shows reliance on selling inventory. Note too high may mean cash is idle.

left.title: Current ratio
points: Can the firm meet debts due in a year?

right.title: Acid test ratio
points: Inventory may be slow to sell

teach.heading: Check: ratio
teach.note: Answer D. Markup is on cost: 30,000/60,000 = 50%. Option A uses sales.

check.q: A shop buys goods for 60,000 pounds and sells them for 90,000. What is the markup?
check.why: Profit is 30,000; 30,000 divided by the 60,000 cost = 50%. Dividing by sales gives the margin of 33.3%.

teach.heading: Using ratios to decide
bullets: Compare with last year and with rivals
Look for causes: price, costs, inventory
Ratios use past data and ignore non-financial factors
teach.note: Evaluate Meridian: gross margin up 2 points, operating margin down 2 points, acid test 0.75. A bank might hesitate to lend more. Possible actions: control expenses, reduce inventory, negotiate supplier terms. In the exam, conclude with a judgement and supporting numbers, and mention that more information is needed. Honest interpretation matters: ratios must not be used to mislead lenders or investors.

practice: Sales 250,000, gross profit 90,000, operating profit 30,000. Calculate both margins.
Current assets 90,000, inventory 40,000, current liabilities 50,000. Calculate current and acid test ratios.
State two limitations of ratio analysis.
independent: Core: Calculate six ratios for a fictional business from the data provided.
Extend: Explain why a business with a high current ratio may still have poor liquidity.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Using two years of ratios for a fictional shop, decide whether the bank should lend 50,000 pounds. Give a reasoned judgement.
exit: Write the formula for operating profit margin.
What does an acid test ratio of 0.5 suggest?
Big question: how do we know a business is doing well? Name two ratios you would use.
lessons.homework: Take last year's and this year's figures for a business of your choice (given by the teacher) and compare three ratios.
lessons.send: SEND: provide formula cards with a worked example. EAL: simplify vocabulary: profit margin, liquidity. Stretch: investigate the differences between margin and markup.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.1: Economies and diseconomies of scale
lessons.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is it cheaper per item to make a million than a hundred?
objectives: Explain internal economies of scale: purchasing, technical, financial, marketing and managerial
Explain external economies
Explain diseconomies of scale and the limits to growth
successCriteria: All: define economies and diseconomies of scale
Most: give an example of an internal economy and a diseconomy
Some: calculate average cost and evaluate whether a business should keep growing
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: industrial clusters; Maths: average and unit cost
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair treatment of suppliers and workers when a business has bargaining power

keywords.def: a fall in average cost as output rises
a rise in average cost as a business grows too large
total cost divided by output
getting a lower price by buying large quantities
a cost saving that arises from the growth of the business itself
a cost saving arising from the growth of the industry or area

starter: Calculate gross profit margin: gross profit 60,000, sales 200,000.

teach.heading: Average cost and scale
bullets: Average cost = total cost divided by output
Growth may spread fixed costs over more units
Economies of scale lower average cost
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Nile Noodles Ltd. Output 10,000 packs, total cost 80,000: average cost 8 pounds. Output 40,000, total cost 240,000: average cost 6 pounds. Ask pupils to explain why. Misconception: total costs still rise; only the cost per unit falls.

teach.heading: Worked example: spotting the economy
teach.note: Model the calculation and its meaning. Ask pupils what causes the saving: spreading fixed costs, buying in bulk. Ask what happens at 100,000 packs if average cost rises to 6.50: diseconomies.

model.problem: Nile Noodles produces 10,000 packs at a total cost of 80,000 pounds and 40,000 packs at 240,000 pounds. Calculate the fall in average cost and the percentage fall.
model.answer: Average cost falls by 2 pounds, a 25% fall

teach.heading: Internal economies
teach.note: Table with causes and a Nile Noodles example. Technical: a bigger machine producing more per hour. Managerial: specialist managers. Financial: lower interest as the firm is seen as safe. Marketing: one advert spread over many sales. Purchasing: bulk discount.

head: Economy
Cause
Example
rows: A packing line that runs faster
Banks lend to a large firm at a lower rate
One national advert for all products

teach.heading: External economies
bullets: Skilled labour pool in an area
Benefit all firms in the industry or area
teach.note: Use the fictional Westgate Textile Quarter: many textile firms in one area mean colleges train sewing staff and suppliers open nearby. Contrast with internal: external is outside any one firm's control. Ask pupils how they differ from internal economies in how they arise.

teach.heading: Diseconomies of scale
bullets: Workers feel less valued, motivation falls
teach.note: Ask: when might Nile Noodles be too large? Staff feel like numbers; decisions are slow. Remedies: decentralise, improve communication, create smaller teams. Link to organisation structure from earlier.

teach.heading: Check: economy or diseconomy?
teach.note: Answer B. Falling motivation and slow communication raising costs is a diseconomy. A and C are economies.

check.q: As a firm doubles in size, communication slows and workers become less motivated, so average costs rise. This is:
check.why: Rising average costs from poor communication or motivation are diseconomies of scale.

practice: Total cost 150,000 for 30,000 units. Calculate average cost.
Name two internal economies of scale.
Explain one reason for diseconomies of scale.
independent: Core: Sort ten statements into economies, external economies and diseconomies.
Extend: Explain how bulk buying lowers average costs.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Nile Noodles plans to double output. Discuss whether this will definitely reduce its average cost, using at least one economy and one diseconomy.
exit: Define economy of scale.
Calculate average cost: total 90,000, output 15,000.
Big question: why is a million cheaper per item than a hundred? One reason.
lessons.homework: Find a large business and list two ways it benefits from size.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a card sort. EAL: pre-teach bulk and average. Stretch: link economies to market share and pricing.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.2: Production, lean production and technology
lessons.title: Production methods and productivity
lessons.bigQuestion: Should a business make one at a time or make thousands?
objectives: Describe job, batch and flow production
Compare labour-intensive and capital-intensive methods
Calculate productivity and the effect of improving it
successCriteria: All: name three production methods
Most: match methods to products
Some: calculate productivity and judge an improvement
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: manufacturing methods; Maths: rates and percentage change
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair treatment of workers when machines replace jobs; responsibility to retrain

keywords.def: making one-off items to a customer's order
making a group of identical items one batch at a time
continuous mass production of identical items
uses many workers relative to machinery
uses lots of machinery relative to workers
output per worker or per input over a period

starter: What causes a diseconomy of scale?

teach.heading: Three methods
teach.note: Bismillah. Table, then ask pupils to place the examples: a wedding dress, a batch of 200 loaves, a bottle of water on a factory line. Job: skilled, high price, flexible but slow. Batch: moves between products. Flow: cheap per unit but inflexible and costly to set up.

teach.heading: Labour-intensive and capital-intensive
bullets: Capital-intensive: many machines, e.g. car plant
Choice depends on product and costs
Technology often shifts firms towards capital
teach.note: Discuss which suits a business offering personal service and which suits a high-volume product. Note a firm can be capital intensive with few workers but needs expensive equipment. Link to Unit 5.3. Ask how rising wages would affect the choice.

teach.heading: Worked example: productivity
teach.note: Show productivity as output divided by number of workers (or hours). Calculate the percentage change. Ask what happens to labour cost per unit when productivity rises. It falls if wages do not rise as fast.

model.problem: Orchard Bakeries produced 4,800 loaves a day with 12 workers. After buying a new mixer it produces 5,400 loaves with 12 workers. Calculate the productivity before and after, and the percentage increase.

teach.heading: Check: method
teach.note: Answer C. Making identical products continuously is flow.

check.q: A factory makes millions of identical plastic bottles without stopping. Which method is this?
check.why: Continuous production of standard goods is flow production. Batch would stop between batches.

teach.heading: Improving productivity
teach.note: Link back to training and motivation. Ask pupils for the effect on unit cost and competitiveness. Evaluate a decision: a 40,000 pounds machine that raises output 12.5 per cent; compare with the extra revenue. Remind pupils to refer to the business.

practice: A firm makes 7,200 items with 18 workers. Calculate productivity per worker.
State one benefit and one drawback of flow production.
Explain why a tailor uses job production.
independent: Core: Classify six fictional products by production method and say why.
Extend: Explain the effect on unit cost of a rise in productivity.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Orchard Bakeries can invest 60,000 pounds to move from batch to flow production. Evaluate using flexibility and cost per loaf.
exit: Define productivity.
Name the three methods.
Big question: one at a time or thousands? One condition for each.
lessons.homework: Compare how two products in your home were likely made and name the method.
lessons.send: SEND: provide picture cards for methods. EAL: pre-teach batch, flow. Stretch: investigate how mass customisation blends methods.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.2: Production, lean production and technology
lessons.title: Lean production, just-in-time, Kaizen and technology
lessons.bigQuestion: Can a business be cheaper by wasting less?
objectives: Explain lean production and its aim of making effective use of resources
Describe just-in-time and Kaizen
Evaluate technology such as robotics: cost, productivity, quality and flexibility
successCriteria: All: define lean production, JIT and Kaizen
Most: explain benefits and risks of JIT
Some: evaluate investing in robotics for a given business
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and Computing: automation and quality control
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste and caring for the environment; fair treatment of workers affected by automation

keywords.def: methods that reduce waste and use resources effectively
receiving supplies just as they are needed, holding little inventory
continuous improvement through small changes by all staff
using programmable machines to perform tasks
resources, time or materials that add no value
ability to change output or products quickly

starter: Calculate output per worker: 900 units, 15 workers.

teach.heading: Lean production
bullets: Use space, labour and stock efficiently
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Marwan Motors. Ask pupils to list wastes in a factory: faulty parts, waiting, unused stock, excess movement. Islamic ethics warn against wastefulness as a general value; the teacher can expand without quoting. Lean means more from less, not less quality.

teach.heading: Just-in-time
teach.note: Compare benefits and risks. JIT: parts arrive just when needed. Saves storage space and money tied up in inventory. Risk: if a supplier is late the line stops. Needs reliable suppliers and good communication. Ask: which would suffer in a lorry strike? Use the compare layout.

left.title: Benefits of JIT
points: Little inventory, so lower storage costs

teach.heading: Kaizen
bullets: Continuous improvement by small, regular changes
Motivates workers; benefits build over time
teach.note: Give the example: a worker at Marwan Motors suggests moving a toolbox, saving 20 seconds per car, 400 cars a day = 8,000 seconds, about 2.2 hours. Link to Herzberg: recognition and responsibility. Limitation: slow gains and needs a culture where staff are listened to.

teach.heading: Worked example: robotics decision
teach.note: Model investment appraisal at simple level. Ask about non-financial factors: staff jobs, quality, flexibility, breakdown risk. A robot may do the same work as three staff but needs servicing and cannot change tasks easily.

model.problem: A robot costs 150,000 pounds and replaces 3 workers each paid 28,000 a year. Servicing costs 12,000 a year. Calculate annual saving and the payback time.
model.answer: Saving 72,000 a year; payback about 2.1 years

teach.heading: Check: JIT
teach.note: Answer D. JIT reduces inventory but increases dependence on suppliers.

check.q: Which is a risk of just-in-time production?
options: A late delivery can stop production
check.why: With little inventory held, a delay in supply can halt production.

teach.heading: Technology: judging the balance
bullets: Flexibility: can it adapt to new products?
Effect on workers: redundancy and retraining
teach.note: Ask pupils to give both sides. Bring in the human angle: workers who lose jobs need fair treatment, retraining and honest communication. Then evaluate: robots suit high volume, repeated tasks; labour suits variety. Final judgement should refer to the business's volume and finance.

practice: Calculate the annual saving of a machine that saves 2 workers at 25,000 each and costs 8,000 a year to service.
Explain what Kaizen is.
State one benefit and one drawback of using robots.
independent: Core: Match six actions (reducing inventory, staff suggestion scheme, automating welding) to lean, JIT, Kaizen or technology.
Extend: Explain two reasons why a firm using JIT needs good suppliers.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): A fictional furniture firm making custom designs considers buying robots. Should it? Give a reasoned judgement.
exit: Define just-in-time.
Name one drawback of robotics.
Big question: can a business be cheaper by wasting less? One example.
lessons.homework: Find an example of a business that uses technology to improve productivity and explain one benefit and one problem.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a labelled flow diagram for JIT. EAL: pre-teach Kaizen with a picture. Stretch: investigate the ethics of automation.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.3: Factors of production; Unit 5.4: Quality
lessons.title: Factors of production and quality
lessons.bigQuestion: What do you need to make anything, and how do you make sure it is good?
objectives: Describe enterprise, capital, land and labour and how their relationships change
Explain quality for goods and services
Explain quality control, total quality management and quality as competitive advantage
successCriteria: All: name the four factors of production and define quality
Most: compare quality control with TQM
Some: judge whether a business should invest in TQM
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: resources; Science: testing and measurement
lessons.smsc: Moral: ihsan (doing work with excellence) and honesty about product quality; the teacher may expand without quotation

keywords.def: the resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital, enterprise
money and equipment used in production
natural resources and the place where production happens
checking products at the end or during production to remove faults
all staff responsible for quality at every stage
something that makes a business better than rivals

starter: Name one method of lean production.

teach.heading: Four factors
bullets: Enterprise: the risk-taker who organises production
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Palm Grove Dates farm. Land: the orchard; labour: pickers; capital: sorting machine; enterprise: owner Karim who decides what to grow and takes risk. Ask: what would happen if one factor is missing? Each earns a reward: rent for land, wages for labour, a return for capital, profit for enterprise. Note that many Muslims avoid interest-based finance as a widely held position; the teacher may expand on how a return on capital can be structured differently, without giving rulings.

teach.heading: How the mix changes
bullets: Rising wages push firms to use machines
Some firms stay labour-intensive for personal service
Services often rely on skilled labour more than land
teach.note: Ask: how does Palm Grove change when a machine picks dates? Fewer workers, higher capital. A capital-intensive method needs more investment but may lower unit cost. A labour-intensive business like a tailoring shop may stay labour-intensive because customers value personal work.

teach.heading: Quality and why it matters
bullets: Good: fit for purpose, reliable, safe
Fewer returns, complaints and repeat jobs
teach.note: Ask pupils what 'quality' means for a date farm (fresh, clean, correctly graded and labelled) and for a taxi service (punctual, safe, polite). Honesty in labelling and weighing is a form of quality; the teacher may expand on ethics. Link to the Islamic ethos of excellence in work without quoting texts.

teach.heading: Control and TQM
teach.note: Compare. Quality control: inspectors check and reject, finding faults after they happen. TQM: everyone checks their own work, aims to prevent faults. Costs: TQM needs training and culture change; control needs inspectors and wastes rejected products. Ask pupils which saves more in the long run.

teach.heading: Worked example: cost of poor quality
teach.note: Model the calculation to show why quality matters. Ask what other costs exist not in the sum: reputation, lost customers.

model.problem: Palm Grove packs 20,000 boxes a year. 3% are returned as damaged. Each returned box costs 4.50 pounds to replace and refund. TQM would cut returns to 1% and costs 2,000 pounds a year. Is TQM worthwhile on cost alone?
model.answer: Net loss of 200 pounds on cost alone; but reputation benefits may justify it

teach.heading: Check: TQM
teach.note: Answer B. TQM puts everyone in charge of quality. A describes quality control.

check.q: Which statement describes total quality management?
options: Inspectors check items at the end of the line
All staff are responsible for quality at every stage
The business reduces prices to attract customers
Only managers decide on quality standards
