check.why: TQM spreads responsibility for quality across all staff to prevent faults. Option A is quality control.

teach.heading: Quality as competitive advantage
bullets: Customers pay more for reliable goods
Reputation spreads by word of mouth
Harder for rivals to copy than low price
But quality costs money; the price must reflect it
teach.note: Evaluate: should Palm Grove compete on quality or price? Quality may justify higher prices and loyalty; but customers on low income may prefer cheap dates. Remind pupils that a reasoned answer uses the business's market.

practice: A firm makes 50,000 items, 2% are faulty and each costs 3 pounds to replace. Calculate the cost.
Name the four factors of production and the reward for each.
Explain one difference between quality control and TQM.
independent: Core: Match six examples (a tractor, a farmer, a field, a worker, an owner) to factors of production.
Extend: Explain two benefits of quality to a restaurant.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Is quality the best way for a small fictional bakery to beat a supermarket? Give a judgement.
exit: List the four factors.
Define quality control.
Big question: what does a business need to make anything, and how does it keep it good?
lessons.homework: Choose a product you own, and list the factors of production used to make it and one quality check.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture cards for factors. EAL: pre-teach capital with examples. Stretch: link TQM to Kaizen.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.5: Business and the international economy
lessons.title: Globalisation, multinationals and exchange rates
lessons.bigQuestion: Who wins and who loses when a business goes global?
objectives: Explain globalisation, with opportunities and threats
Explain benefits of multinationals to the firm and benefits and drawbacks for host countries
Calculate exchange rate conversions and explain how exchange rate changes affect importers and exporters
successCriteria: All: define globalisation and multinational and convert a currency
Most: explain benefits and drawbacks of a multinational for a host country
Some: evaluate the effect of an exchange rate change on competitiveness
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: globalisation and development; Maths: ratio and proportion
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair treatment of workers abroad and honest trade across borders

keywords.def: the growing connection of businesses and markets around the world
a business with operations in more than one country
the country where a multinational operates but is not based
the price of one currency in terms of another
a business that buys goods or services from abroad
a business that sells goods or services abroad
how attractive a business's prices and products are compared with rivals

starter: Name the four factors of production.

teach.heading: What is globalisation?
bullets: Trade, people and ideas move easily across borders
Cheaper transport and the internet help
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Orion Foods: it buys spices from one country, processes in another and sells in six. Ask for opportunities and threats for a small local firm: larger market but competitors with lower prices. Ask pupils to think of products in their home made abroad. Do not give statistics unless supplied.

teach.heading: Multinationals and host countries
teach.note: Compare. Benefits to the firm: new markets, cheaper labour and materials, avoiding trade barriers, spreading risk. Host country benefits: jobs, tax, skills, infrastructure. Drawbacks: profits sent abroad, pressure on local firms, low wages or environmental harm if poorly regulated, jobs lost if the firm leaves. Use the fictional Orion factory in Tamar.

teach.heading: Exchange rates
teach.note: Teach conversion as multiplication or division. For the exercise assume £1 = 1.25 US dollars and £1 = 60 Egyptian pounds (invented rates for practice). Ask: to convert pounds to dollars, multiply; dollars to pounds, divide. Check the answer is sensible: fewer pounds than dollars.

model.problem: Using £1 = 60 Egyptian pounds (EGP), convert (a) £250 to EGP and (b) 9,000 EGP to pounds.

teach.heading: Effects of exchange rate changes
bullets: Stronger pound: imports cheaper, exports dearer
Weaker pound: exports cheaper, imports dearer
Exporters gain competitiveness when their currency weakens
Importers gain when their currency strengthens
teach.note: Use a UK exporter selling a machine for £10,000. At £1 = 1.25 dollars the US buyer pays 12,500 dollars; at £1 = 1.50 dollars they pay 15,000 dollars: dearer, fewer sales. Ask pupils what happens to an importer buying in dollars. Remember the direction by working through an example each time.

teach.heading: Check: exchange rate
teach.note: Answer C. A stronger pound makes UK goods cost more abroad. A is a weaker pound.

check.q: The pound becomes stronger against the dollar. What is the likely effect on a UK exporter selling to the USA?
options: Its goods become cheaper for US customers
Its goods become more expensive for US customers
check.why: A stronger pound means US buyers need more dollars per pound, so UK goods cost more and exports may fall.

teach.heading: Judging globalisation
bullets: Consider the size of the firm
Consider worker conditions and the environment
Honest dealing: fair prices to suppliers
Reach a reasoned conclusion for the business
teach.note: Practise evaluation. Ask: should a small local bakery welcome a foreign supermarket arriving? Mixed: lower prices for customers, but threat to jobs. Link to ethics: fair wages and honest contracts matter wherever a firm operates; the teacher can expand using the class's knowledge.

practice: Convert £400 to dollars at £1 = 1.25 dollars.
Convert 3,000 EGP to pounds at £1 = 60 EGP.
State two benefits of a multinational to a host country.
independent: Core: Complete a conversion table for five prices using £1 = 1.25 dollars and £1 = 60 EGP.
Extend: Explain how a weaker pound affects an importer of coffee beans and an exporter of cars.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Orion Foods plans to open a factory in Tamar. Discuss the effect on Tamar and on Orion, and judge whether it is a good idea.
exit: Define globalisation.
Which currency movement helps exporters?
Big question: who wins and who loses when a business goes global? One of each.
lessons.homework: Check the labels of five items at home and note where each was made; discuss what globalisation means for them.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a conversion method card (multiply or divide). EAL: pre-teach host country with a map. Stretch: explain why the exchange rate changes.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.6: Government objectives and policies; Unit 1.7: External factors
lessons.title: Government and the external environment: policies, tax and STEP factors
lessons.bigQuestion: How can decisions made by governments and society change a business overnight?
objectives: Explain government objectives, spending, taxation, legislation, trade policy and interest rates
Explain the effect of interest rate changes on businesses and consumers
Analyse social, technological, environmental and political influences
successCriteria: All: name three government policies and one effect on business
Most: explain how a rise in interest rates affects a business and its customers
Some: evaluate how an external change would affect a given business
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: sustainability; Computing: technology; Citizenship: government and law
lessons.smsc: Moral: obeying the law, paying tax honestly, caring for the environment (stewardship)

keywords.def: money collected by government from people and businesses
a tax on imported goods
the cost of borrowing or the reward for saving, as a percentage
roads, rail, power and communications that support business
laws passed by government that businesses must follow
social, technological, environmental and political influences

starter: Name one benefit of a multinational to a host country.

teach.heading: What governments do
bullets: Spend on public services and infrastructure
Raise taxes to pay for spending
Pass laws to protect workers and consumers
Set trade policy, such as tariffs and trade blocs
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional country of Zandia. Governments want economic growth, jobs, stable prices and safe consumers. Ask: how can a new road help a business? Lower transport costs, better access to customers. Ask: how can higher tax hurt? Lower profit or higher prices. Teacher: do not discuss real governments' policies as facts; keep fictional.

teach.heading: Tariffs and taxes
teach.note: Model a tariff calculation. Ask who pays: the importer, who may pass it on to customers. Limits: a government cannot spend more than it raises without borrowing; high tax may reduce enterprise. Point out how a business pays taxes honestly and on time as a matter of trust.

model.problem: Zandia imposes a 10% tariff on imported bicycles. Samir imports 200 bicycles at 120 pounds each. Calculate the tariff and the new cost per bicycle.
model.answer: Tariff 2,400 pounds; cost per bicycle 132 pounds

teach.heading: Interest rates
teach.note: Compare effects of a rise in rates. Businesses with loans pay more; customers who borrow spend less; savers may save more. So demand falls for expensive goods bought on credit. A fall helps borrowers. Then the Islamic note: many Muslims avoid interest-based borrowing, so interest rates may affect them differently; the teacher may expand on the position without ruling.

teach.heading: STEP factors
teach.note: Give examples for Zandia: an ageing population increases demand for care homes (social); AI tools change office work (technological); a plastic ban affects packaging (environmental); a new government changes tax rules (political). Ask pupils to name one threat and one opportunity for a bakery from each factor. These influence decisions such as location, product and price.

teach.heading: Check: tariff
teach.note: Answer D. A tariff raises the cost of imported goods. A and B are not tariff effects.

check.q: What is the most direct effect of a tariff on an importer?
check.why: A tariff is a tax on imports so the importer's costs rise.

teach.heading: Evaluating external change
bullets: List the factor and who it affects
Assess how big the effect is
Recommend action: adapt, absorb, or change plans
teach.note: Practise on a scenario: a rise in interest rates from 4% to 7% on a 50,000 pounds loan: interest cost rises from 2,000 to 3,500. Discuss action: cut costs, raise prices, overpay loan. Reach a decision. A business that adapts survives; one that ignores change may fail.

practice: Loan of 80,000 pounds. Interest rate rises from 5% to 8%. Calculate the extra annual interest.
Name one STEP factor and its effect on a clothes shop.
Explain how a new road could help a business.
independent: Core: Sort ten events into social, technological, environmental or political.
Extend: Explain two effects of a tax rise on a restaurant.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Zandia raises interest rates and introduces a plastic packaging ban. Which is more serious for a small food manufacturer, and why?
exit: Define tariff.
State one effect of an interest rate rise on consumers.
Big question: how can decisions made by governments or society change a business overnight? Give one example.
lessons.homework: Find one news story that affects businesses and classify it as a STEP factor.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a STEP sorting grid. EAL: pre-teach tariff, legislation. Stretch: weigh short-term against long-term effects.

lessons.title: Business success and failure
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you know when a business has really succeeded?
objectives: Describe measures of success: revenue, market share, customer satisfaction, profit, growth, owner and employee satisfaction
Explain reasons for failure: cash flow, lack of finance, being uncompetitive, failure to adapt
Make a reasoned judgement on a business's success
successCriteria: All: name four success measures and two causes of failure
Most: calculate revenue growth and profit margin to measure success
Some: evaluate a business using several measures and reach a conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: English: structured argument and evaluation; Maths: percentage change
lessons.smsc: Moral: success judged by honest earning, fairness and service, not only by profit

keywords.def: achieving a business's aims and objectives
when a business cannot continue or achieves poor results
how well customers' needs and expectations are met
an increase in the size of the business, such as sales or number of outlets
to change in response to new conditions

starter: State one effect of a rise in interest rates on a business.

teach.heading: Measures of success
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Kite Cafe. Ask pupils: if Kite Cafe makes 20,000 profit but staff are unhappy and customers complain, is it successful? Draw out that success can be judged by different measures and different stakeholders. Link to Islamic ethos: honest and fair dealing matter beyond profit; the teacher may expand.

teach.heading: Worked example: measuring success
teach.note: Model with two years of data. Ask: which stakeholder cares about each measure? Evaluate: revenue growth is good but the profit margin fell, suggesting costs rose faster. Pupils should comment on both.

model.problem: Kite Cafe: Year 1 revenue 200,000, profit 30,000. Year 2 revenue 240,000, profit 33,600. Calculate revenue growth and profit margin each year.
steps: Compare: revenue up but margin down
model.answer: Revenue grew 20%; margin fell from 15% to 14%

teach.heading: Why businesses fail
bullets: Cash flow problems or lack of finance
Uncompetitive: prices or quality worse than rivals
Failure to adapt to changing tastes or technology
teach.note: Link to earlier units: cash flow forecasts, market research, location. Give Kite Cafe's story: a rival opens opposite with cheaper coffee, but Kite does not respond and delays paying suppliers: cash shortage. Ask how it could have avoided failure. Honest early warnings to lenders and suppliers is better than hiding problems.

teach.heading: Success or failure: the evidence
teach.note: Table to use as an evaluation template. Pupils use evidence from each measure. Note some measures may conflict: profit up but customer satisfaction down. A final judgement must say which measure matters most for that business and why.

teach.heading: Check: reason for failure
teach.note: Answer B. Not responding to changes is failure to adapt. A and C are strengths.

check.q: A video shop keeps renting DVDs while customers move to streaming, and closes. This is mainly:
check.why: Ignoring changes in customers' behaviour and technology is failure to adapt.

teach.heading: Writing an evaluation
bullets: Link to the business and its aims
Weigh the measures against each other
teach.note: Model the structure for 20-mark questions: point, evidence, explanation, counter-point, judgement. Tell pupils that the examiner wants a decision supported by evidence, not a list. Use Kite Cafe: a conclusion could be 'Moderately successful, because revenue and profit are growing, but customer and staff satisfaction need attention for long-term survival.'

practice: Revenue rose from 150,000 to 183,000 pounds. Calculate the percentage growth.
State two reasons why a business might fail.
Explain why profit alone may not show success.
independent: Core: Use a data table for a fictional business to complete five success measures and judge each.
Extend: Explain why customer satisfaction matters for long-term success.
Stretch: Evaluate (20-mark style plan): 'Profit is the best measure of a business's success.' Plan an answer with two points for, two against and a conclusion.
exit: Name three measures of success.
State one reason for business failure.
Big question: how do you know a business has really succeeded? Answer with one measure and one reason it might mislead.
lessons.homework: Choose a local business and write a short paragraph judging its success, using two measures.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a writing frame for evaluation. EAL: vocabulary support for success measures. Stretch: write a full 20-mark answer.
